records.name: CAR
records.current_summary:
In the Cordillera administrative region, inter-tribal customary justice runs alongside the formal system: the Kalinga bodong/pagta peace-pact system — with its own holders, sanctions and authority over crimes and tribal-related offences — was codified in February 2026 by the provincial government into a 137-page written Pagta, a step its sponsors present as recognition by the national courts. Academic documentation frames this as legal pluralism in which customary resolution of criminal and tribal offences operates with police, prosecutors and local officials participating, and constitutional recognition of indigenous justice extends across the country's autonomous regions.

No trans-specific bodong ruling, customary exclusion or punishment relating to gender expression appears in this record. The finding for a visitor is structural uncertainty — which forum decides a dispute — without any evidence of a trans-specific adverse outcome: the customary system here is a civil and restorative-justice institution with no criminal-law expansion over morality documented, which keeps it a marginal concern, not a threat finding.

sources.claim: Academic journal article on the bodong/pagta customary justice system in Kalinga: framed in legal-pluralism and restorative-justice theory, it documents bodong holders resolving criminal and tribal offences alongside the formal justice system, with Philippine National Police personnel, prosecutors and barangay officials participating in customary-law conflict resolution.

sources.title: Kalinga (province) - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's article on Kalinga, a landlocked province within the Cordillera Administrative Region whose capital Tabuk was established when it was formed out of Kalinga-Apayao on 8 May 1995 by Republic Act No. 7878, documents the province as a long-standing flashpoint between the Marcos martial-law government (declared September 1972) and its indigenous peoples over the Chico River Dam Project, which would have displaced about 100,000 indigenous people, with the 24 April 1980 murder of tribal leader Macli-ing Dulag turning public opinion and making the dam dispute a landmark ancestral-domain case study in the country. It records the September 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord that created the Cordillera Autonomous Region and notes that attempts to ratify actual autonomy failed in plebiscites. For this record it frames the province's indigenous governance context in which the customary bodong/pagta justice system the summary concerns operates; it does not itself discuss the bodong/pagta codification.

sources.title: Cordillera Administrative Region - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's region framework page for the jurisdiction itself: the Cordillera Administrative Region was created on 15 July 1987, comprises six provinces (Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province) centred on Baguio, is the country's only landlocked region and, per the 2020 Census of Population and Housing, the least populated in the country with fewer residents than the national capital. It describes the region as home to numerous ethnic groups, including a majority-Igorot province, and records a living Cordillera autonomy movement alongside the earlier Cordillera People's Liberation Army ceasefire secured by the Aquino government. A framework document for the jurisdiction in which the record's customary-justice claims sit, with the region itself as the subject.

freshness_all.fact: Codification of the Kalinga 'Pagta'/bodong peace-pact system confirmed (launched Feb 2026) but the cited bworldonline article now 404s; replaced by contemporaneous coverage.

newer.title: Kalinga launches codified 'Pagta' peace pact (Daily Tribune)
How Kalinga turns a peace pact into a living festival (Rappler)

records.name: Daejeon
records.current_summary:
In October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo, holding the military should have considered her a woman when reviewing fitness for duty — a ruling widely described as a landmark in the case brought to repeal the discharge decision.

On 24 June 2024, after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's original 'natural death' classification and recognised the 2021 death as service-related, Byun was interred at the National Cemetery in Daejeon. Around 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, arguing her service did not qualify her for interment there: state recognition of a trans person at the national memorial ground, met with a small but public rejection in open space.

sources.claim: Yonhap (2021-10-07): Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's discharge of the late Ssg. Byun Hee-soo — the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier — holding the military should have treated her as female after her legal sex change, that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal, and that fitness review should weigh basic rights. Decision vindicated the posthumous appeal. For the record: dated, court-level proof that a Daejeon court delivered a pro-recognition ruling on trans military status.

Aju Press (2024-06-25): Korea's first transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024 — some 60 activists protested, arguing the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment; she died by suicide in 2021 after the forced 2020 discharge (gender dysphoria classified as mental disorder, post-surgery physical-disability finding) and court appeals. For the record: her Daejeon state burial stands as official honouring contrasted with the still-conservative institutional stance.

records.name: North Chungcheong
records.current_summary:
North Chungcheong (capital: Cheongju) is scored −0.02 below the national 0.71 on the basis of the Byun Hee-soo case and its institutional aftermath, with the single-incident caveat applied explicitly. Byun, 23, was found dead in her Cheongju home on 3 March 2021 (apparent suicide) following forced military discharge and during ongoing mental-health counselling at a centre near her residence. Initial police and Army handling classified the death as 'natural'; this was overturned only three years later (April 2024) when the Ministry of National Defense's Central Military Casualty Review Board recognised it as service-related. The wrongful initial classification is the evidence: it reflects an institutional denial of the connection between anti-trans policy and a trans person's death, corrected only after sustained advocacy.

Per the single-incident rule, one death cannot establish a Cheongju pattern, and no repeat violence data exists for this unit. It is included at −0.02 rather than zero because Chungcheongbuk-do is small enough for one nationally prominent case to carry weight, and because the institutional response (wrongful classification sustained for three years before correction) is a state-implicated finding. Compared to Daejeon (0.69), which hosts the positive court ruling that corrected the same institution's error, North Chungcheong's share of the Byun story is purely negative—but the deviation is identical because the correction (Daejeon court, MND board) already mitigates the initial harm.

sources.claim: BBC (2021-03-03): Byun Hee-soo, 23 — South Korea's first transgender soldier, discharged for gender-affirming surgery, landmark military challenge rejected July 2020 — was found dead at her home in Cheongju, North Chungcheong province (counsellor raised the alarm after 28 Feb); her death triggered national debate on treatment of trans troops. For the record: the single incident the region's −0.02 deviation rests on, dated and located in Cheongju.

PinkNews (2021-03-04): after Byun Hee-soo was found dead in Cheongju on 3 March 2021, public grief and demands for LGBT protections surged — National Human Rights Commission honoured her, prosecutors and activists called for an anti-discrimination bill (8th introduction since 2007; June 2020 draft included gender-identity provisions); society-wide 'responsibility' discourse followed. For the record: aftermath evidence — no new regional law, but documented national-protection pressure arising from this province's incident.

records.name: South Chungcheong
records.current_summary:
South Chungcheong (Chungcheongnam-do) was swept into the same provincial fight over student human-rights protections that engulfed Seoul, but with the institutions on opposite sides: on 24 April 2024 the provincial council passed a bill to repeal the Chungcheongnam-do Student Human Rights Ordinance (in force since 10 July 2020; its Article 15 stipulates non-discrimination obligations based on gender identity and sexual orientation), and the provincial Office of Education sued to overturn it, obtaining a suspension of the repeal's execution from the Supreme Court on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in effect. On 21 February 2025 the Chungcheongnam-do and Seoul offices of education filed a joint response to a communication from three UN special procedures, appearing as 'stakeholders (enforcing authorities)' in the repeal dispute still pending before the Supreme Court and opposing the rollback on constitutional and treaty grounds.

The evidence is primarily resident-facing (student non-discrimination rules), carrying small weight for a traveler under the scoring rules; no traveler-facing enforcement action, arrest, or event obstruction is documented for this unit. The −0.02 deviation below the national 0.71 was set on the premise that the province's education office aligns with the repeal campaign; the source shows the opposite alignment - the elected council moved against SOGI protections while the enforcing education office defended them in court and won a suspension - so the record reads as mixed (a hostile council initiative, a protective institutional response) rather than one-directionally de-protective, and the deviation direction should be reviewed accordingly. No other province-specific incident or enforcement series was identified for this unit.
records.current_localsOnly: The ordinance battle - the council's April 2024 repeal bill and the education office's successful court challenge - bears on enrolled students and school staff in public offices, not on visitors.

sources.claim: Republic of Korea response (21 February 2025) to the Joint Communication from UN Special Procedures (ref. OL KOR 3/2024) on the student human-rights ordinances, filed by the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education as 'stakeholders (enforcing authorities)' in the repeal dispute pending before the Supreme Court. The Chungnam section records: the provincial council passed a repeal bill on 24 April 2024 against the ordinance enacted 10 July 2020 (Article 15 covers gender identity and sexual orientation); the Office of Education challenged it before the Supreme Court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in effect; it argues the repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties. The Seoul section records its 11 July 2024 petition against the council's abolition and the Supreme Court's 23 July 2024 suspension.

sources.title: Ordinance of Student Rights (Wikipedia article on South Korea's student human rights ordinances)
sources.claim: The English Wikipedia article on South Korea's student human rights ordinances lists South Chungcheong Province (Chungcheongnam-do) among the jurisdictions that adopted the framework, enacting its ordinance in 2020, and records that the province's ordinance was later revoked in 2024 - matching the 24 April 2024 provincial-council repeal vote this record documents. It describes the framework the ordinance belonged to: these ordinances prohibit discrimination of students by gender, religion, nationality, disability, race and sexual orientation, with the provisions on gender and sexual diversity named the most contentious items. It corroborates this record's timeline of a Chungcheongnam-do student human rights ordinance in force from 2020 (the record dates it from 10 July 2020) through the 2024 repeal fight.

records.name: Gyeonggi
records.current_summary:
The model student human-rights ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province; Seoul's office adopted it in 2012 and it spread to other regional offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave.

When Seoul's metropolitan council — pushed by a campaign begun by religious and parents' coalitions in August 2022 — abolished the capital's ordinance on 26 April 2024, Gyeonggi stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher warned that wholesale abolition 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector'. The province's standing is thus origin-and-retention of student protections rather than any enforcement measure aimed at visitors.
records.current_localsOnly: The protections credited to Gyeonggi - the 2010-origin student rights ordinance it continues to enforce - bear on enrolled students and school staff, not on visitors.

sources.claim: Korea Times report (28 April 2024) on the Seoul Metropolitan Council's abolition of the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it: the ordinance model was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province'; abolition was pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six regional education offices - Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the (Seoul) superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.

sources.title: Ordinance of Student Rights (Wikipedia article on South Korea's student human rights ordinances)
sources.claim: The English Wikipedia article on South Korea's student human rights ordinances records that the framework 'first began in Gyeonggi-do Province (2010)' and that the Gyeonggi-do and Seoul ordinances are the only two to include the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy, the Gyeonggi ordinance also covering sexual orientation and gender identity - the provisions most disputed in the 2024-26 repeal wave. It adds that in Gyeonggi-do the Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights and that Gyeonggi-do dedicates a day to Student Human Rights Day. The article corroborates this record's origin claim that Gyeonggi enacted the model ordinance first, in 2010, with sexual-orientation and gender-identity non-discrimination among its protections.

records.name: RegiÃ³n de TarapacÃ¡
records.current_summary:
The Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman, holding that Chile's "femicide" (femicidio) offence — the strongest gendered-violence protection in the penal code — covers only "a person biologically female" and therefore the conviction could not stand as framed. The case: Yuri Pizarro, a 55-year-old trans woman whose body was found on the southern coast of the provincial capital in June 2022; her killer, Jhonatan Cañon, had been convicted at first instance to presidio perpetuo, and on the defence's nullity motion the Iquique court declared the sentence void in early October 2023. This is a named judicial finding that, in this region, the most severe legal protection available for gender-motivated violence does not extend to trans women. The annulment occurred in Tarapacá, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction. Tarapacá accounted for 1.56 % of the national anti-LGBTI case total in 2024, a small-share region in which a single structural finding dominates the per-capita signal.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.08 deviation. The legal framework is unchanged (Law 21.120 and the femicide article remain on the books nationally), but the regional judiciary's operative interpretation in this instance creates a concrete protection gap for a trans person who is assaulted in Tarapacá. Compared with La Araucanía (0.65), Tarapacá is 0.01 lower: Araucanía's −0.07 is trend-based (+150 % rise, low visibility), whereas Tarapacá carries a specific court ruling that names trans women as outside the femicide definition. Compared with Arica y Parinacota (0.69), Tarapacá is 0.05 lower because the Iquique annulment is a documented finding within Tarapacá's own judicial district, whereas Arica's deviation rests on the shared northern-court context with no trans-specific incident of its own.

sources.claim: Chilevisión (5 Oct 2023): the Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the trial of Jhonatan Cañon for the 2022 murder of trans woman Yuri Pizarro in Tarapacá, holding that Chile's femicidio offence covers only 'a person biologically female' and so the conviction could not stand as framed — voiding the strongest gendered-violence conviction available. Annulled in Tarapacá, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction.

Movilh XXIII annual report (Mar 2025, 2024 data): Tarapacá held about 2% of nationally documented homo/transphobic cases and ranked among the fastest-rising regions (+18.18% year-on-year, with growth also flagged at +19.51% in the period tables) — the dataset basis of the record's case-share claim, which no region-specific source covers (rule 5).

records.name: RegiÃ³n de Magallanes y AntÃ¡rtica Chilena
records.current_summary:
In 2024 a trans woman, Kenia Chacón, was the victim of an attempted femicide (femicidio frustrado) in Punta Arenas. The tribunal imposed four years of internación parcial against the five years of internación total requested by the prosecution; the victim's mother publicly denounced devaluation of the attack on the basis of her daughter's gender identity. In April 2026 the regional director of SernamEG (the national women and gender-equality service) publicly criticised the sentence as not reflecting the gravity of the attack and announced an appeal — a named institutional pushback that partially offsets the judicial under-penalisation. Magallanes also appeared among the regions with the largest percentage increases in the 2024 dataset and holds 0.96 % of the national case total.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.06 deviation. The under-sentencing for gender-motivated violence against a trans woman is a concrete traveler-relevant severity finding; the SernamEG appeal is a genuine institutional counter-signal that prevents a deeper deduction. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Magallanes is 0.02 higher: Tarapacá's Iquique court annulment voids the femicide protection entirely for trans women in that jurisdiction, whereas Magallanes applied the femicide framework but under-sentenced, and the state service is actively appealing to correct the record.

For a visitor, the practical exposure in Magallanes is low absolute case volume (0.96 % of the national total) but the judicial precedent of reduced sentences for attacks on trans women is a severity signal that moves the region below national.

sources.claim: BioBioChile/El Pingüino (15 Apr 2026): SernamEG announced it will appeal the sentence in the attempted femicide (femicidio frustrado) case of trans woman Kenia Chacón, attacked in Punta Arenas in 2024 — challenging the four-year internación parcial imposed against the five years of internación total the prosecution had sought; the victim's mother publicly denounced the devaluation of the attack based on her daughter's gender identity.

Movilh XXIII annual report (Mar 2025, 2024 data): Magallanes held 0.96% of the national case total and was among the regions with the largest percentage increases (+100% year-on-year) — the dataset basis of the record's share and rise claims, which no region-specific source covers (rule 5).

records.name: RegiÃ³n de Arica y Parinacota
records.current_summary:
Arica y Parinacota is grouped with Tarapacá in the dossier under the heading "the northern courts' non-recognition of trans women as women," reflecting the shared judicial geography of northern Chile. However, the specific Iquique Court of Appeals annulment was delivered in Tarapacá, and Arica's own data contribution is limited to a 0.84 % share of national cases (2024). No trans-specific incident, court ruling, or enforcement failure originating in Arica was identified. The deviation below national rests on the shared northern judicial-climate framing and the broader pattern — reported for both the 2024 and 2025 Movilh annual surveys — that homo/transphobia cases rose in most regions outside the metropolitan core.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.03 deviation, the smallest in the scored set. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Arica is 0.05 higher because it lacks the concrete femicide-annulment ruling; the northern-court context applies but is not evidenced with a named local finding. Compared with Ñuble (0.67), Arica is 0.02 higher: Ñuble's +300 % surge is a more specific and dramatic statistical signal than Arica's sub-percent case share.

For a visitor, the practical exposure in Arica is not materially different from the national baseline; the small deduction reflects the dossier's explicit grouping under "worse than national" and the absence of any positive institutional finding (no diversity office, no municipal ordinance, no documented court protection).

sources.claim: Chilevisión crime report: the Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman after holding that Chile's "femicide" offence protects only "a person biologically female," so the conviction could not stand as framed — a northern-court finding that the country's strongest gendered-violence protection does not extend to trans women. The dossier cites it as the basis for grouping Tarapacá and Arica y Parinacota as worse-than-national on shared judicial geography; the ruling itself is Tarapacá's.

Movilh's XXIII Annual Human-Rights Report on Sexual and Gender Diversity (2024 data, published March 2025), full per-region table: 2,847 recorded cases nationally (+78.7 %), with Arica y Parinacota holding a 0.84 % share — among the lowest in the country — in a year that saw increases in 11 of 16 regions; small-share regions where a single case dominates the rate.

sources.title: Las denuncias por casos de discriminación a comunidad LGTBIQ+ aumentan en Arica y Parinacota
sources.claim: Movilh's annual rights report covering 2021 (published April 2022) showed Chile-wide homophobia/transphobia complaints and cases falling 12%, the first drop in eight years, but in five regions they rose and Arica y Parinacota was one of them: its reports climbed around 300% against 2020. The piece ties the national decline to the visibility won by the sexual-diversity movement in the year equal marriage was approved (2021). For this record it evidences the region's own complaint trajectory running against the national trend — concrete regional data backing the dossier's grouping of the northern regions as worse than national.

sources.title: Arica se convierte en el cuarto territorio donde Iguales presta apoyo legal gratuito en casos de discriminación por orientación sexual y/o identidad de género
sources.claim: On 14 November 2017 Fundación Iguales announced that Arica became the fourth territory where it provides free legal aid for discrimination cases based on sexual orientation and/or gender identity, via a collaboration agreement with pro-bono lawyer Piera Balbontin Nef covering Arica's jurisdiction. The foundation's legal director said discrimination is greater in regions far from the capital, which is why local legal support matters. For this record it documents that an accessible local channel for anti-LGBTI discrimination complaints exists in the region itself — a concrete mitigation resource for a visitor facing an incident, complementing the national anti-discrimination framework.
